source.title: Towards Atoms of Large Language Models
source.authors: Chenhui Hu; Pengfei Cao; Yubo Chen; Kang Liu; Jun Zhao

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses neuron polysemanticity and reports measurements of faithfulness and structural stability, but those measures do not directly test whether neurons respond to unrelated inputs or contexts, nor do they test the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports neurons' and features' faithfulness and stability as candidate-atom criteria. These are related structural measures, not direct measurements of polysemantic responses, so the rows are linked to none of the claim versions. Its monosemanticity evaluation concerns atoms and SAE features, not neurons; cited examples and results from prior work are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study motivates its work with neuron polysemanticity but never measures how often or how strongly neurons respond to unrelated inputs. Its neuron result is a structural stability score (q* = 0.5%), a coherence/sparsity criterion from compressed sensing. The authors read low q* as implying polysemanticity, but q* is a different construct from semantic response mixing, so it belongs under fits_no_version. The LLM-judge monosemanticity test (Fig. 6, Fig. 45) scores only SAE features and the authors' atoms, not neurons. The paper also never says whether its 'neurons' are MLP neurons or coordinates of the residual-stream activations it extracts.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors find neurons perfectly faithful but structurally unstable, which they take as implying polysemanticity, and SAE features more stable but unfaithful. Their TSAE atoms reach R² ≈ 99.9% and q* ≈ 99.8% and score higher on an LLM-judged monosemanticity test, which excludes neurons.
record.recipe_differences: Uses AIP-based faithfulness and stability criteria on language-model representations, with threshold-activated sparse autoencoders; it does not reproduce the original visual analysis of InceptionV1 neuron activations.

fits_no_version.finding: Neurons reach R² = 1 but only q* = 0.5% stability (coherence/sparsity criterion), averaged over layers of Gemma2-2B, Gemma2-9B and Llama3.1-8B. The authors interpret this as implying polysemanticity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Taken as a basis for sparse decomposition of entity-token activations, neuron coordinates fail a compressed-sensing uniqueness criterion almost everywhere. This is a structural, not semantic, indicator of polysemanticity.

fits_no_version.finding: GemmaScope/LlamaScope SAE features reach q* = 68.2% but R² = 48.8% on the same entity activations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Off-the-shelf SAE features are more structurally stable than neurons but reconstruct entity activations poorly.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: The neuron results are aggregate across models and layers, and the reported stability metric is not a direct semantic or response-based polysemanticity measure. The paper's monosemanticity judge evaluation does not score neurons.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible claim-version results left out. The paper's atom and feature monosemanticity scores are not neuron results; the figure reports these graphically, with no text-stated numeric values for the scores.

untested.parts: No rate of MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts, and no layer-wise semantic measure for neurons. Neurons are scored only by structural stability q*, averaged across layers.
Superposition is assumed as background, citing Elhage et al. and Hu et al. Fig. 34 is said to show superposition in activations, but no causal link to neuron polysemanticity is tested.
Neuron polysemanticity is not compared across activation functions, architectures or regularization. The JumpReLU versus ReLU comparison concerns SAE dictionaries, not model neurons.
Measurement dependence of neuron polysemanticity judgments is not examined.

record.verdict_notes: R² = 1 for neurons is trivial: any full basis reconstructs the activations exactly. Activations are taken at the final subject token, apparently from the residual stream, so 'neurons' may not be MLP neurons. Results are given only as averages over layers and models. The neuron finding is presented as consistent with Olah et al. (2020), an original source, but is not a test of it.

versions.untested_parts: Vision models and InceptionV1 neuron responses.
Direct rates or measurements of MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts, including variation across layers.
Whether polysemanticity is caused by representing more sparse features than there are neurons and packing them together.
Polysemanticity arising from initialization, regularization, or training noise when capacity is sufficient.
Changes in the share of polysemantic neurons across activation functions, architectures, or regularization, and whether that share can be reduced without substantial performance loss.
Whether canonical polysemantic neurons detect a shared feature or related jobs, making truly unrelated mixtures rare.
Whether neuron polysemanticity judgments vary with activation range or explanation-scoring method.
